summaries.Q511: Housed in the former Saint-Pierre abbey on place des Terreaux, this museum, founded in 1801, long included a flower room for the designers of the Lyon silk industry. It holds The Stoning of Saint Stephen, Rembrandt's earliest known painting, and in 1901 became the first museum outside Paris to buy works by the Impressionists.
summaries.Q509: Buried in the slope of the Fourvière hill, this museum designed by Bernard Zehrfuss and opened in 1975 unfolds its collections along a concrete ramp spiralling downwards. On show are the Claudian Tablet, the Coligny calendar and a bust of Caracalla handed over by the Louvre: the emperor was born in Lugdunum.
summaries.Q8397: This mansion in Old Lyon, fitted out in the early 16th century, was occupied by the Gadagne family, bankers of Florentine origin whose fortune inspired the saying "as rich as Gadagne". It houses the Lyon history museum, opened in 1921, and the puppet arts museum, built around the original Guignol puppet.
summaries.Q8330: Located since 1995 at the Cité Internationale, near the parc de la Tête d'Or, the macLYON occupies a Renzo Piano building that preserves the façade of the former Lyon trade fair palace. Its policy of producing works required the architect to provide a completely modifiable interior, suited to each exhibition scenario.
summaries.Q3330146: Founded by the Chamber of Commerce and opened in 1864, this museum, housed since 1946 in the hôtel de Villeroy, holds more than 2.5 million textiles covering 4,000 years of the history of fabric. Threatened with break-up from 2014, it was saved in 2017: the two mansions were transferred to the region for a symbolic one euro.
summaries.Q3279836: In the Croix-Rousse, this venue created in 1970 by the weavers' cooperative Cooptiss brings back to life the world of the canuts, the district's silk workers. Guided tours, with a weaving demonstration on a Jacquard handloom, retrace the history of Lyon silk since 1536, from the silkworm cycle to the canut revolts.
summaries.Q8323: Created in 1964 by the printer Maurice Audin and the book historian Henri-Jean Martin, this museum occupies the hôtel de la Couronne, a late 15th-century building where the aldermen of Lyon sat from 1604 to 1655. Its displays run from the origins of printing to the information society; a working letterpress workshop has been installed there since 1988.
summaries.Q3330257: Founded in 2005 by the miniaturist Dan Ohlmann in the former Maison des Avocats on rue Saint-Jean, this private museum brings together two collections: one devoted to the art of the miniature, the other to film special effects, with twelve rooms showing animatronics, models, costumes and sets, including those from the film Perfume.
summaries.Q1516: Built from 1872 after the vow that placed Lyon under the protection of Mary during the war of 1870, this neo-Byzantine basilica is the work of Pierre Bossan. On 8 December 1852, the unveiling of the gilded statue of the Virgin on the neighbouring bell tower saw the people of Lyon light small candles: the Festival of Lights was born.
summaries.Q1521: Seat of the archbishop of Lyon, primate of the Gauls, Saint-Jean cathedral was built from 1175 to 1480, a project begun in Romanesque style and finished in Gothic. It holds a 14th-century astronomical clock, restored in 2021, and, out of attachment to the Lyon rite, was the last cathedral in France to acquire an organ, in 1841.
summaries.Q3246: Consecrated in 1107 by Pope Paschal II, this abbey church is one of the few Romanesque churches preserved in Lyon. Turned into a grain store during the Revolution, which spared it from destruction, it reopened for worship in 1802. The four columns of the transept crossing are thought to be reused from the altar of the federal sanctuary of the Three Gauls.
summaries.Q8250: Rebuilt in the 14th and 15th centuries in Flamboyant Gothic, Saint-Nizier was the church of the common people and burghers of Lyon, facing a cathedral that gathered the elites. It owes its name to bishop Nizier, who died in 573 and whose body drew crowds. Its parish register has made it possible to observe the beginnings of the Black Death in Lyon in 1348.
summaries.Q8600: The church of the Lyon charterhouse until the Revolution, Saint-Bruno is one of the city's few Baroque religious buildings. Its 18th-century dome, funded by the Consulate on condition that it be visible from the centre of Lyon, rises to 50 metres. Inside, the baldachin designed by Servandoni was meant to magnify the presence of Christ.
summaries.Q5278: Erected in 12 BC on the slopes of the Croix-Rousse, this sanctuary brought together each year, from 1 August, the delegates of the Gaulish nations for the worship of Rome and Augustus. In 1528, a cloth merchant found in his vineyard the lower part of the Claudian Tablet, a bronze plaque engraved with the speech given by the emperor Claudius in 48.
summaries.Q10181: The site was occupied as early as the 6th century by a place of worship founded by Sacerdos; restored around 800 by Leidrade, the church took the name of Saint George and gave the district its name. Attached from 1315 to the commandery of the Knights of Saint John of Jerusalem, it was rebuilt in neo-Gothic style by Pierre Bossan in 1844-1845.
summaries.Q8238: The church of the Cordeliers friary, it received the body of cardinal Bonaventure, who died in Lyon in the middle of the council on the night of 14 to 15 July 1274. Consecrated unfinished in 1328 and completed around 1484, it is the only medieval building remaining in the north of the 2nd arrondissement. Pope Francis raised it to the rank of minor basilica in 2019.
summaries.Q9528: A church attested as early as the 9th century in documents passed on by bishop Leidrade to Charlemagne. The Romanesque parts, begun in the second half of the 12th century, were finished in the 13th, then supplemented with Gothic elements in the 15th and 16th centuries. The stone spire, destroyed in 1817, was replaced in 1875 by a wooden one.
summaries.Q1531: Built from 1863 to 1864 on quai Tilsitt in a neo-Byzantine style, it is the work of the young architect Abraham Hirsch, who later became the official architect of the city of Lyon. Twelve columns, recalling the twelve tribes of Israel, separate the nave from the aisles; the organ comes from the basilica of Saint-Martin d'Ainay, sold in 1864.
summaries.Q10182: A former Oratorian church, begun in 1665 and completed in 1670, its façade by Toussaint-Noël Loyer dates only from 1756. It became a parish church in 1791 and took the name of Saint Polycarp, mentor of the first two bishops of Lyon. The façade still bears the scars of the cannon fired by the Convention on the Croix-Rousse in 1793.
summaries.Q2957338: Built from 1617 to 1622 by the Jesuit brother Étienne Martellange for the collège de la Trinité, this Baroque church housed, from 1702, the first astronomical observatory in Lyon, built above its pediment. Napoleon presided there over the Consulta of Lyon in January 1802; deconsecrated in 1920, it now serves as a concert hall.
summaries.Q3124: At the foot of the Croix-Rousse, this amphitheatre belonged to the federal sanctuary where the sixty Gaulish nations celebrated the worship of Rome and Augustus. Given in AD 19 by an aristocrat from Saintes and enlarged to about 20,000 seats, it was, according to historians, the site of the execution of Christian martyrs, including Blandina, in 177.
summaries.Q1510: Set against the Fourvière hill, this theatre, built at the beginning of the Empire, perhaps under Augustus, could hold up to 10,000 spectators after its enlargement. Buried and forgotten in the Middle Ages, it was uncovered from 1933 by works employing up to 120 labourers, and became a stage again in 1946 with Aeschylus's The Persians.
summaries.Q9496: The Grand Théâtre of 1831 shows only eight muses on its attic storey: for lack of space, Urania was never made. Jean Nouvel restructured it between 1989 and 1993, keeping only the façades and the foyer beneath a glass roof rising to 42 metres; breakdancers have been training under its arcades since the 1990s.
summaries.Q4221: A theatre has stood since 1792 on the site of the Célestins friary, founded in 1407. Gaspard André's Italian-style auditorium, inaugurated in 1877, burned down in 1880 and reopened in 1881, rebuilt exactly as before. In May 68, stagehands hid there for a year part of the antiquities of the Egyptology institute of the University of Lyon.
summaries.Q3175: Next to the large theatre on the Fourvière hill, this odeon of about 3,000 seats hosted music, public readings and meetings; in Gaul, only Vienne also has such a pair. Its ruins, known in the Middle Ages as the Grottoes of the Saracens, were long taken for the amphitheatre of the martyrs, before the clearing work begun in 1941.
summaries.Q8426: Nicknamed the Twenty-Four Columns, this neoclassical courthouse built by Louis-Pierre Baltard from 1835 to 1847 lines the Saône in Old Lyon. Its great hall, 17 metres high, was fitted out as an assize court with 750 seats for the trial of Klaus Barbie, convicted in July 1987 of crimes against humanity.
summaries.Q8592: Nothing remains of this castle perched on a rocky spur some fifty metres above the Saône: the fortress was demolished in 1793. The residence of the archbishops of Lyon, it became a state prison under Louis XI and saw the passage of Ludovico Sforza, Cinq-Mars and the marquis de Sade, who stayed there in 1768.
summaries.Q17319801: In the former cloister of the Benedictine abbey that became the fine arts museum, this garden was laid out as an open-air sculpture museum from 1883. It holds Rodin's The Shade, a bronze cast in 1904 with deliberately unfinished hands, around a fountain crowned by an Apollo.
summaries.Q10144: Commissioned by Bordeaux, which then gave it up, this fountain by Bartholdi, made by the workshops of the Statue of Liberty, was bought by Lyon after the 1889 Universal Exposition and unveiled on place des Terreaux in 1892. Amphitrite drives four sea horses whose nostrils breathe out a spray of water.
summaries.Q10147: On 800 m2 of blank wall beside the Saône, this trompe-l'œil painted in 1994-1995 by CitéCréation places twenty-four famous figures from Lyon at the windows, the rule reserving the upper floors for the dead; on the ground floor, contemporaries such as Paul Bocuse and Frédéric Dard mingle with passers-by.
summaries.Q3259169: The longest of the traboules in Old Lyon, as its name indicates: it links 27 rue du Bœuf and 54 rue Saint-Jean, crossing four separate buildings and punctuated by several small successive courtyards. It is open to the public.
summaries.Q16303800: This 24-tonne quartzite is an erratic block, carried from the Alps to Lyon by glaciers. In 1890, workers digging the trench for the Croix-Paquet funicular struck this rock, which proved impossible to break. Once extracted, it was set up in 1891 at the end of the boulevard de la Croix-Rousse; it is one of the symbols of the district.
summaries.Q625: 101 metres high, this tower raised for the 1894 Lyon Universal Exposition recalls the third level of the Eiffel Tower; a rumour attributes it to Gustave Eiffel, who had nothing to do with it. A lift carried 22 people up to the viewpoint for 1 franc. Bought in 1953 by the RTF, it serves as a relay antenna and is closed to the public.
summaries.Q8412: In 1704, a block carved with a bull's head was found in a Fourvière vineyard: an altar commemorating a taurobolium, a sacrifice in honour of the goddess Cybele held on 9 December 160 for the health of the emperor Antoninus Pius, then ill. It is kept at the Gallo-Roman museum along with other altars of the same cult.
summaries.Q3368319: In 1780, the Saône was crossed here on a chain of twelve boats, the pont Volant. The present footbridge, opened in 1983 after years of campaigning by local residents, hangs its 136-metre span from a single inverted-Y mast painted red. It was named in 2024 in honour of the prosecutor general Pierre Truche.
summaries.Q3368281: Ice on the Saône carried away the first two bridges built here, in 1643 and then in 1711. The present footbridge, opened to the public at the end of 1832, held up better: together with the Homme de la Roche footbridge, it is the only bridge in Lyon that the Germans did not destroy during their retreat of 2 September 1944.
summaries.Q3396474: Between Bellecour and Saint-Jean, a wooden bridge crossed the Saône as early as 1642. The pont Tilsitt replaced it in 1807, was rebuilt in 1863-1864, then blown up by the German forces in September 1944. The present bridge, three reinforced concrete arches faced with Hauteville stone, was built from 1946 to 1950 and named Bonaparte in 1964.
summaries.Q3991: Opened in 1857, the same year as Central Park in New York, this 117-hectare park designed by the Bühler brothers owes its name to a legend: a treasure including a golden head of Christ was said to be buried there. The digs carried out until 1860 turned up nothing; the lake, the zoo and the botanical garden, on the other hand, are certainly there.
summaries.Q8668: Heir to the botanical garden opened in 1796 at the convent of la Déserte, on the slopes of the Croix-Rousse, it moved in 1857 to the parc de la Tête d'Or; the orangery was carried there and rebuilt stone by stone. It presents 15,000 taxa over 8 hectares, including 6,500 m2 of glasshouses, and its herbarium holds about 213,000 specimens.
summaries.Q8670: Jules Senis, a tiler and mason who had fled the Spanish Civil War, vowed to build a garden if his cancer went into remission. From 1958 he dedicated to his mother Rosa Mir this 400 m2 courtyard whose columns are covered with thousands of shells, Catalan in inspiration, in the manner of Gaudí. It has been listed as a historic monument since 1987.
summaries.Q3162538: A gift from the city of Montreal for the twentieth anniversary of its cooperation with Lyon, this 6,000 m² garden on the heights of Saint-Just has been open since August 2001. Six chair-sculptures by Michel Goulet, fixed to the ground, stand beside a small bridge that recalls the Jacques-Cartier bridge in Montreal.
summaries.Q2387471: Created in 1858 at the instigation of prefect Vaïsse, this municipal zoo in the parc de la Tête d'Or presents a little over 300 animals of 66 species over 9 hectares, freely open and free of charge since the outset. The African plain, opened in 2006, brings giraffes, zebras and flamingos together over 2.5 hectares.
summaries.Q9504: This urban park at Fourvière links the area around the basilica to the Loyasse cemetery by a belvedere walkway. Its Quatre-Vents footbridge follows the route of a line opened in 1900, on which trams fitted with a hearse trailer carried passengers and coffins to the cemetery; the service closed in 1938.
summaries.Q614: At 63,000 square metres, it is the largest square in Lyon and its kilometre zero. A first statue of Louis XIV, melted down in 1793 to make cannon, was replaced in 1825 by Lemot's equestrian work: cast in Paris, it was hauled here in twelve days by a team of twenty-four horses.
summaries.Q1506: Its name is said to come from the Latin Terralia, the ditch that lay here until the 16th century. The Bartholdi fountain, a triumphal chariot of the Garonne originally commissioned by Bordeaux in 1857, was bought by Lyon in 1890 and unveiled in 1892. In 1994, the artist Daniel Buren and the architect Christian Drevet redesigned the square with 68 mini-fountains.
summaries.Q764519: The "hill that prays" is where the Roman colony of Lugdunum was founded, in 43 BC. Its name comes from the Latin forum vetus, the old forum, which stood on the site of the forecourt of the basilica, built from 1872 to 1884. On a clear day, the view reaches as far as Mont Blanc, 160 km away.
summaries.Q8220: Cut through under the Second Empire at the initiative of prefect Vaïsse under the name rue Impériale, this shopping street, nicknamed the rue de la Ré, took its present name in 1878. At number 22, a red paving stone and a plaque recall the assassination of president Sadi Carnot by the anarchist Caserio, on 24 June 1894.
summaries.Q10169: Called place Confort until 1782, it takes its name from the Jacobins, the Dominican friars who occupied the south side of the square. Its fountain, designed by Gaspard André and unveiled on 14 July 1885, carries statues of Hippolyte Flandrin, Gérard Audran, Guillaume Coustou and Philibert Delorme.
summaries.Q9518: It owes its name to the Célestin friars, established from 1407 to 1778 on a former Templar estate. Redesigned between 1993 and 1995 during the building of an underground car park, it holds a kind of telescope devised by Daniel Buren, which gives a kaleidoscopic view of the car park.
summaries.Q9516: The oldest square in Lyon serves as the forecourt of the Saint-Jean primatial church; in 1794, the Revolution had renamed it place du Temple de la Raison. Its fountain of 1844, designed by René Dardel, reproduces a small ancient temple sheltering a Saint John the Baptist baptising Christ, sculpted by Bonnassieux.
summaries.Q8226: Cut through in stages from 1817 to 1841 to link place Carnot to Bellecour, the former rue de Bourbon took its present name on 26 May 1885, only four days after the death of Victor Hugo. Dug up in 1974 for the building of metro line A, it became on 8 December 1976 the second pedestrian street in Lyon.
summaries.Q4376: This narrow paved street, famous for its bouchons, owes its name to the chestnut trees that once lined the neighbouring place Bellecour and were removed in the 18th century; the consular act dates from 30 September 1723. At 3 bis, Roger Planchon founded the théâtre de la Comédie in 1952 in a former locksmith's workshop.
summaries.Q3390131: Laid out on the site of the convent of la Déserte, demolished in 1813, the square honours Fay de Sathonay, mayor of Lyon from 1805 to 1812. Its two fountains are decorated with cast-iron lions from Le Creusot, replicas of those of the fontaine de l'Institut in Paris. The bronze statue of sergeant Blandan, which disappeared during the war, was replaced by a stone one in 1961.
summaries.Q11029: Attested as early as the 13th century, it was the main street on the left bank of the Saône, then the street of booksellers and printers in the 16th century, home in particular to the workshop of Sébastien Gryphe. Long insalubrious and rehabilitated in the 1980s, it has become a stronghold of Lyon cooking, with its bouchons and restaurants.
summaries.Q3126137: Opened in February 1971 at La Part-Dieu, they replaced the former Cordeliers market hall, demolished in January of the same year. Nicknamed the belly of Lyon, this market of 13,500 square metres brings together some sixty traders; it was renamed in 2007 in tribute to Paul Bocuse, who bought supplies there for his restaurants.
summaries.Q4013: Heir to a hospice attested in 1184 near the Rhône bridge, this hospital had Rabelais as a doctor from 1532. Its façade on the Rhône, designed by Soufflot, was built from 1741 to 1761. Closed in 2010 and then listed as a historic monument in 2011, it now houses a hotel, shops and the cité de la gastronomie.
summaries.Q1992: Built to the plans of François-Alexis Cendrier and brought into service in 1856, the station was inaugurated on 2 June 1857. In 1896, the Société Lumière shot two short films there, including Arrival of a Train at Perrache. A Shoah memorial, recalling the convoys of deportees that left from there, was unveiled nearby in January 2025.
summaries.Q2016: Opened on 17 January 1876 with the line to Montbrison, this station at the foot of Fourvière was the headquarters of the Compagnie des Dombes et des chemins de fer du Sud-Est. Beyond its points, the tracks run into the Loyasse tunnel, 1,417 metres long. Since 2012 it has been the terminus of the two tram-train lines of western Lyon.
summaries.Q5270: Built from 1972 to 1977 by the American practice Araldo Cossutta, this skyscraper of 164.9 metres, a cylinder topped by a transparent pyramid, was given the nickname the Pencil by the people of Lyon. Its architect wanted its top to come roughly to the height of the Fourvière basilica. A hotel occupies the upper floors.
summaries.Q2970872: Brought into service on 6 September 1900, this ficelle climbs in two minutes from Old Lyon to the Fourvière basilica: 427 metres long for 116 metres of height difference, almost entirely in a tunnel beneath the forecourt. In 1932, a car that had run out of control struck a building below, without causing any casualties.
summaries.Q8484: Built on a former fortification of the Lyon defensive belt, the lunette des Charpennes raised in 1842, the lycée was created in 1914: it served as a barracks and then a hospital during the First World War, and the first normal school year only took place in 1919. Édouard Herriot taught there; the school takes its name from the neighbouring parc de la Tête d'Or.
summaries.Q8399: A medieval and Renaissance district at the foot of Fourvière, it brings together Saint-Georges, Saint-Jean and Saint-Paul. Looked down on in the 19th century, a "dead district" according to Louis Boitel in 1833, long under threat of demolition, it was protected by its designation as a conservation area in 1964 and is today a Unesco heritage site.
summaries.Q516: Built from 1646 to 1672 under the direction of Simon Maupin, it was then reckoned the largest city hall in France; damaged by fire in 1674, it was restored to the plans of Jules Hardouin-Mansart. On its door of 1651, a knocker showing a child knocking with his bottom is nicknamed Tony Tape-du-Cul.
summaries.Q8213: Inaugurated on 25 August 1860 by Napoleon III and the empress Eugénie, this building designed by René Dardel today houses the Lyon chamber of commerce and industry. It was on leaving the building, on 24 June 1894, that president Sadi Carnot was assassinated by the anarchist Caserio: a red paving stone marks the exact spot.
summaries.Q8422: Laid out at the end of the 3rd century, when the inhabitants of Fourvière, left without water, came down to build a district beside the Saône, it leads to the cathedral from which it takes its name. Its traboules are numerous: the longest in Old Lyon starts at no. 54 and crosses four houses to 27 rue du Bœuf.
summaries.Q8696: This climb up the Croix-Rousse counted 705 looms in 1788 and was taken by the demonstrators of the canut revolt in 1831. At no. 95, the first French consumer cooperative was founded in 1835; in 1895, Marius Berliet tested his first car there, the Pantoufle, which ended up in a pork butcher's window.
summaries.Q3462254: One of the three parishes of Old Lyon, along with Saint-Jean and Saint-Paul, named after its church. The Hospitallers of Saint John of Jerusalem settled there in 1315; their commandery, demolished in 1860, gave way to the square that bears its name. On rue du Doyenné stands the statue of Laurent Mourguet, the creator of Guignol.
summaries.Q8324: This covered passage, rebuilt from 1825 by the architect Vincent Farge and reopened in 1828, takes its name from the argue, a tool for drawing gold and silver wire. Its rotunda has seen three statues of Mercury in succession: the first stolen in 1902, the second melted down by the Germans during the war, the third stolen in 1995 and then again in 2011.
summaries.Q8352: Set at the tip of the Presqu'île, at the confluence of the Rhône and the Saône, this museum designed by Coop Himmelb(l)au opened in December 2014 after an eventful construction: estimated at 61 million euros in 2000, it finally cost 330. Inside are the Choulans mammoth, found in 1859, and an example of Sputnik 2.
summaries.Q3151766: Created in 1982 in the Monplaisir district, where the Lumière brothers devised the Cinematograph that filmed Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory in Lyon in 1895, the institute preserves and shares the heritage of cinema. Its collection of 1,425 Lumière films has been on Unesco's Memory of the World register since 2005.
